States and diagrams

A state line fixes the state of a fluid from two properties, and Dome finds the rest. Each section below starts from a sheet you can copy into Dome, shows what Dome gives, and then lists the rules. The sheets follow Help › Examples › States and properties (water).

Fixing a state

Water is heated at 15 bar from a compressed liquid at 50 °C to a superheated vapor at 320 °C. This sheet fixes four states along the way and finds the heat transfer per unit mass.

fluid water
p_b = 15 [bar]
state 1 : p = p_b, T = 50 [C]
state 2 : p = p_b, x = 0.3
state 3 : p = p_b, h = 2200 [kJ/kg]
state 4 : p = p_b, T = 320 [C]
q_14 = h_4 - h_1

At the right of each state line, Dome shows the phase, or the quality of a two-phase state: x_3 = 0.696. It gives h_1 = 210.7 kJ/kg, h_4 = 3082.5 kJ/kg and q_14 = 2871.8 kJ/kg.

  1. A fluid line sets the fluid of the state lines after it.
  2. state 1 : p = p_b, T = 50 [C] fixes state 1 from two of p, T, v, u, h, s and x. It defines p_1, T_1, v_1, u_1, h_1, s_1 and x_1, which any line may use.
  3. Each property needs its unit, as a number in an equation does. A value may be a number, a variable or an expression.
  4. A value may be an unknown that another line finds. In state 2 : p = 0.1 [bar], s = s_1, s_1 comes from state 1.
  5. A label may be a number or a name: state 2s : … defines p_2s, h_2s and the rest.
  6. x has a value only for a two-phase state, saturated liquid and vapor included. A line that uses x_1 of the compressed liquid above is an error.
  7. A state of another fluid names it in parentheses: state 3 (water) : …. Two fluids shows a sheet with states of two fluids.
  8. The States tab of the results lists every state's phase and properties, in the units chosen in the header. The two properties given on each state line are in bold. With states of more than one fluid, it also lists each state's fluid (Two fluids).
  9. The copy button at the right of the States tab copies the table as tab-separated text. File › Export › States table writes it as a CSV file.

The shot shows the whole example, with a T–s diagram of the four states.

Property functions

A property function gives one property at a state that need not be numbered, such as the saturated liquid and vapor at the boiler pressure.

p_b = 15 [bar]
T_sat = Tsat(water, p = p_b)
h_f = h(water, p = p_b, x = 0)
h_g = h(water, p = p_b, x = 1)
h(water, T = T_x, x = 0) = 100 [kJ/kg]

Dome gives T_sat = 198.29 °C, h_f = 844.63 kJ/kg, h_g = 2791 kJ/kg and T_x = 23.828 °C.

  1. Write the fluid first, then two named properties: h(water, p = p_b, x = 0).
  2. The functions are p, T, v, u, h, s, x, cp, cv and rho.
  3. Tsat(water, p = …) is the saturation temperature and psat(water, T = …) the saturation pressure. M(water) is the molar mass, 18.015 kg/kmol. M() also gives the molar mass of hydrogen, helium, argon, methane and the other substances of the Reference's list, which Dome has no states for.
  4. Each input needs the unit of its property, as in a state line: h(water, T = 300, x = 0) needs a unit after the 300.
  5. An unknown may be inside a call. The last line finds T_x, the temperature of saturated liquid water with h = 100 kJ/kg.
  6. For an ideal gas, h, u, cp and cv need T alone: h(air, T = 300 [K]) is 300.17 kJ/kg. s needs p as well.
  7. Moist air takes p and two more properties. Moist air gives its functions.

Fluids

A sheet may use several fluids. Here R-134a is compressed from saturated vapor at −10 °C to 8 bar at constant entropy, and the last line reads h of air.

fluid r134a
state 1 : T = -10 [C], x = 1
state 2 : p = 8 [bar], s = s_1
h_air = h(air, T = 300 [K], p = 1 [bar])

Dome gives h_1 = 242.44 kJ/kg, T_2 = 36.926 °C, h_2 = 271.17 kJ/kg and h_air = 300.17 kJ/kg.

Each fluid's h, u and s count from a reference: a state at which the fluid's tables set them to zero. The steam tables set u and s to zero for saturated liquid at 0.01 °C. The R-134a tables set h and s to zero for saturated liquid at −40 °C.

  1. Dome's h, u and s count from the same references as the tables. So h of water and h of R-134a count from different zeros, and a difference of the two has no meaning. Two fluids shows a balance with both.
  2. water, r134a, r134a_book, r22, ammonia and propane have liquid, two-phase and vapor states. Dome's values and the tables, below, says when to write r134a_book.
  3. air, nitrogen, oxygen, carbondioxide and carbonmonoxide are ideal gases with variable specific heats. Their h is zero at 0 K. Air has values from 100 to 3500 K, the others from 220 to 3250 K.
  4. water_ig is water vapor as an ideal gas, with h from 0 K. Its h differs from that of water by a constant, so Dome reports an error where the two meet in one equation.
  5. The h, u and s of an ideal gas are per kg. h(n2, T = 298 [K], p = 1 [atm])*M(n2) is the molar enthalpy, 8663.7 kJ/kmol.
  6. moistair has property functions and no state lines.
  7. A fluid's name may be typed in capitals or lower case. The Reference page lists the other names each fluid accepts, such as h2o and n2.
  8. A name Dome does not know is an error whose message lists the names it knows. When a state is refused shows it.

Dome's values and the tables

A rigid tank holds R-134a at 100 °C. It is cooled until the R-134a is saturated vapor at 20 °C. This sheet finds the heat transfer per unit mass.

fluid r134a
state 1 : T = 100 [C], v = v_2
state 2 : T = 20 [C], x = 1
q = u_2 - u_1

Dome gives q = −68.26 kJ/kg. Worked from the textbook's tables, q is −71.11 kJ/kg. With fluid r134a_book in the first line, Dome gives −71.144 kJ/kg.

Dome's h can differ from the tables' by about 1 kJ/kg, and by up to about 5 kJ/kg in parts of the superheated tables. An answer built from such values can differ by a few percent: in this tank, by 4 %.

For answers that match the textbook's R-134a tables, write fluid r134a_book. Reference gives the differences fluid by fluid, and the range of r134a_book.

Diagrams

A plot line draws the states of the sheet on a property diagram. These two lines draw the four states of the first sheet on a T–s and a p–h diagram.

fluid water
p_b = 15 [bar]
state 1 : p = p_b, T = 50 [C]
state 2 : p = p_b, x = 0.3
state 3 : p = p_b, h = 2200 [kJ/kg]
state 4 : p = p_b, T = 320 [C]
plot Ts : 1 -p- 2 -p- 3 -p- 4
plot ph : 1 -p- 2 -p- 3 -p- 4

Dome draws one figure for each plot line and names it at the right of the line. Each figure has its own tab in the figure pane.

  1. Write plot, the diagram, a colon, and the state labels joined by paths. The diagrams are Ts, Tv, pv, ph and hs.
  2. A path between two labels names the property held constant, as in the table below.
  3. T–v and p–v have v on a logarithmic axis, and p–v and p–h have p on one.
  4. A figure shows the states of one fluid. A state of another fluid gets a note on the figure, such as "state 3 is water; this figure is r134a".
  5. The buttons in the pane's header zoom to a box, fit the view to the data, show data tips and export the figure.
  6. The boxes under the figure show or hide the previous run, the saturation dome, and the isobars (isotherms on p–v and p–h).
  7. Isobars run flat through the dome. Those at the pressures of the figure's states are darker and labelled, so each process at constant pressure lies on a labelled line. Isotherms on p–v and p–h work the same way.
PathProcess
-p-, -s-, -T-, -v-, -h-At constant pressure, entropy, temperature, specific volume or enthalpy. Drawn dashed when that property differs between the two states, as for an expansion with a turbine efficiency.
--A straight line.

Dragging a state

A state on a figure can be dragged when a number in the sheet fixes it along an axis. Here T_4 fixes state 4, and T is the vertical axis of the T–s diagram.

fluid water
p_b = 15 [bar]
T_4 = 320 [C]
state 1 : p = p_b, T = 50 [C]
state 4 : p = p_b, T = T_4
plot Ts : 1 -p- 4

A ring marks state 4 as one that can be dragged. Dragging it up writes a higher T_4 into the sheet, and Dome solves again.

  1. A state can be dragged along an axis when the property it is given on that axis is an input of the sheet.
  2. An input is a line name = number [unit], such as T_4 = 320 [C], or a number written in a state line. T = 320 [C] in the state line works as well.
  3. Dome holds the axes still while the state is dragged. The value moves by as much as the pointer moves from where the drag began.
  4. A state dragged to the edge of the plot stops there. On release, the axes fit the data again, and a second drag goes further.
  5. The new value is written where the number stands in the sheet.

The previous run

After an edit, Dome shows what changed. This is the first sheet with a T–s plot line, after p_b was changed from 15 bar to 30 bar.

fluid water
p_b = 30 [bar]
state 1 : p = p_b, T = 50 [C]
state 2 : p = p_b, x = 0.3
state 3 : p = p_b, h = 2200 [kJ/kg]
state 4 : p = p_b, T = 320 [C]
q_14 = h_4 - h_1
plot Ts : 1 -p- 2 -p- 3 -p- 4

Dome gives q_14 = 2832.2 kJ/kg and shows the change beside the value. The shot shows Help › Examples › States and properties (water) after the same edit.

  1. The edited line is tinted and shows the previous value of the input.
  2. Values that changed show the change beside them. Changed variables and states are tinted in the Workspace and in the states table.
  3. Figures draw the previous run dashed, with a legend naming the change. The Previous run box under the figure shows or hides it.
  4. The previous run is the run from before the edit of the line began. The edit ends when the cursor leaves the line, on Enter, when the sheet loses focus, or after 10 seconds without typing.
  5. A line added that leaves the figure as it was, such as a check line, draws no previous run.

When a state is refused

Each entry gives a sheet, the message Dome shows for it, and what to change.

p and T on the saturation line

fluid water
state 1 : p = 1 [atm], T = 100 [C]

state 1: water: T = 100.00 °C is within 0.15 K of the saturation temperature at 1.013 bar (99.97 °C), where p and T do not fix the state; give x (or v, u, h or s) instead of one of them

At saturation, p and T do not say how much is liquid. Give x in place of T, such as x = 1 for saturated vapor.

A pair that fits two states

fluid water
state 1 : x = 1, h = 2675 [kJ/kg]

state 1: water: x and h fit 2 different states (T = 99.59 °C, p = 0.9996 bar; T = 327.64 °C, p = 124.7 bar); give p or T instead of one of them

Saturated vapor has this h at two pressures. Give the pressure or temperature the problem states in place of h.

A value outside the property data

fluid water
state 1 : p = 15 [bar], T = 2500 [C]

state 1: water: T = 2500.00 °C is above the highest temperature of the property data (1926.85 °C)

Check the value and its unit. The message gives the limit of the data.

A quality outside 0 to 1

fluid water
state 1 : p = 15 [bar], x = 1.2

state 1: quality x = 1.2 is outside 0 to 1

x is a fraction: 85 % is x = 0.85.

One property, or the same one twice

fluid water
state 1 : p = 15 [bar]

state 1 needs exactly two properties; it has 1

Give two different properties. state 1 : p = 15 [bar], p = 10 [bar] gives "state 1 gives p twice".

A missing or unknown fluid

fluid steem
state 1 : p = 1 [bar], x = 1

unknown fluid "steem"; available: water, r134a, r134a_book, r22, ammonia, propane, air, nitrogen, oxygen, carbondioxide, carbonmonoxide, water_ig, moistair

Correct the name to one in the list. A state line with no fluid line above it gets "state 1 has no fluid", with the line to add.

R-134a outside the tables' range

fluid r134a_book
state 1 : T = 220 [C], p = 10 [bar]

state 1: R-134a (book): T = 220.00 °C is outside the range of the textbook's R-134a tables, to which r134a_book is limited (-47.48 to 204.44 °C, up to 39.74 bar); r134a covers it

Write fluid r134a for this state, and for every other R-134a state in the same balance.

Two references for one substance

p = 1 [bar]
q = h(water, T = 100 [C], x = 1) - h(water_ig, T = 100 [C], p = p)

water appears here from the steam tables, h(water, …), and from the ideal-gas model, h(water_ig, …); use one for water in every term: h(water, …) for every water term.

Write every water term with h(water, …). The same holds for R-134a from r134a and r134a_book.

One reference in a balance

Each fluid's h, u and s count from a reference of its own. A balance must take each substance from one reference. Two fluids and Moist air show balances that do, and Reference gives the rules in full.

Moist air

Moist air has a page of its own: Moist air.
